prose.kicker: One elite receiver, four quarterbacks, and a tight end room nobody fixed
prose.title: Real Deal Creel Built a Whole Team and Stopped One Position Short
prose.dek: Keith Creelman rebuilt almost the entire priced lineup in a single offseason, then spent real money at the one spot that still grades badly.

paragraphs: Keith Creelman paid up for Dak Prescott at the Free Agent Auction, put him straight into the starting quarterback slot, and still comes out {{f.team.0008.qb_rank}} at the position. Prescott grades a High-end QB2 and Kyler Murray fills the SuperFlex as a Low-end QB2, which is two solid arms and nothing above them. The overall power rank lands at {{f.team.0008.composite_rank}}.

Receiver is where he actually beats people, and the group grades {{f.team.0008.wr_rank}}. That is Puka Nacua, an Elite WR1, doing most of the lifting: Christian Watson is a Low-end WR3 and Parker Washington a High-end WR3 in a flex. Marvin Harrison Jr, a Low-end WR2, is the best player on the bench, which is a genuinely useful thing to have sitting there.

Saquon Barkley anchors the backfield as a Low-end RB1, with Travis Etienne and TreVeyon Henderson both Low-end RB2s, one in the second running slot and one in a flex. Adequate everywhere, elite nowhere. It grades {{f.team.0008.rb_rank}}.

Dallas Goedert starts at tight end as a Replacement-level TE, and the position grades {{f.team.0008.te_rank}}. Chig Okonkwo is behind him and grades exactly the same, on a current-year salary nowhere near the league minimum. Nothing on this roster fixes it.

Josh Hines-Allen and Jalyx Hunt fill both defensive line slots as Low-end DL2s, Nick Bolton is a Low-end LB2, and Cam Little and Tommy Townsend occupy the kicker and punter slots on salary alone because those slots have no ranking source at all. The priced offense carries {{f.team.0008.studs_current}} studs — Nacua and Barkley — and {{f.team.0008.holes_current}} holes, one of them Goedert. This is a lineup with two edges and two soft spots, not a flat one.

captions.t.0008.lineup: Nacua and Barkley are the edges; Goedert is the part nobody solved.
captions.t.0008.bench: Harrison Jr is real depth. Two of the priciest bench salaries belong to replacement-level players.

paragraphs: Creelman entered the offseason with an active roster of {{f.team.0008.active_roster_opening}}, fewer players than the lineup card has slots. Active salary sat at {{f.team.0008.cap_opening}}. What he was holding was Tetairoa McMillan, TreVeyon Henderson, Christian Watson, Dallas Goedert, Marvin Harrison Jr, Deshaun Watson, Emanuel Wilson, Trey Benson and Keon Coleman, and the priced group among them contained {{f.team.0008.studs_opening}} stud: McMillan, a Low-end WR1.

By the time the Free Agent Auction opened he had already sent McMillan out in the three-way for Puka Nacua and pulled Etienne in from Gride, and the roster stood at {{f.team.0008.active_roster_preauction}} active players. Active salary had climbed to {{f.team.0008.cap_preauction}}. Deshaun Watson, a Replacement-level QB, was still the best quarterback he owned.

Now the roster runs to {{f.team.0008.active_roster_current}} active players. He can field a legal lineup for the first time in the cycle: {{f.team.0008.can_field_lineup_current}}. Cap committed reads {{f.team.0008.cap_current_spent}}.

Holes fell from {{f.team.0008.holes_opening}} to {{f.team.0008.holes_current}}, and the stud count barely moved, which buries the biggest single upgrade of his offseason: the stud slot did not change hands, it changed players, from McMillan to Nacua, a Low-end WR1 becoming an Elite WR1. Prescott replaced Deshaun Watson at quarterback. Barkley replaced nobody, because there was nobody. There is {{f.team.0008.cap_current_room}} of room left, so the building is finished whether he thinks so or not.

Keep the two questions apart. The strength he carried was Henderson, Christian Watson, Goedert and Harrison Jr — those are the only names in the priced starting group that were on hand in the spring. Prescott, Murray, Barkley, Nacua, Etienne and Parker Washington were all created this year, by trade or by auction, which means the team you are looking at is almost entirely an offseason product rather than a holdover.

captions.t.0008.bridge: Three stages, and only the last one has a lineup in it at all.
captions.t.0008.slot_bridge: The names moving through each priced slot say more than the stud count does.

paragraphs: Creelman won {{f.team.0008.era_lots_won}} lots at the Expired Rookie Auction in May. The bill for the lot of them came to {{f.team.0008.era_spend}}. Chris Rodriguez, Kayshon Boutte, Michael Mayer, Will McDonald and Kendre Miller went home with him, and the board scattered fast: Rodriguez was later included in the three-way for Nacua, McDonald and Kendre Miller both became make-room drops on waiver claims, and Boutte and Mayer are the two who ended up with multi-year deals. Cheap tickets, mostly disposable, a couple that stuck.

The Free Agent Auction in late July is where the actual team came from. He won {{f.team.0008.faa_lots_won}} lots there. Spend was {{f.team.0008.faa_spend}}, and Prescott was the top buy at {{f.team.0008.top_buy_price}} — {{f.team.0008.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of his free-agent money, all of it on a High-end QB2. Barkley came off the same board as a Low-end RB1 and Murray as a Low-end QB2, and those two purchases are the difference between a roster and a lineup.

The quarterback shopping did not stop when it should have. Jacoby Brissett grades a Replacement-level QB, cost a long way above the league minimum, and is on the bench next to Deshaun Watson, who grades the same and is at the minimum. Mac Jones came off the same board. Four quarterbacks bought at one auction, and the two who start are a High-end QB2 and a Low-end QB2.
Across the two events the commitment ran to {{f.team.0008.auction_spend}}. One of them built a contender's spine. The other one bought Boutte and Mayer and a lot of paperwork.

captions.t.0008.auction: Two separate auctions, months and an order of magnitude apart.

paragraphs: Creelman restructured Puka Nacua, re-basing the remaining value of an existing deal rather than bolting years onto the back of it, and it is the only Restructure among {{f.team.0008.contracts_count}} contract moves. Everything else was a Multi-Year Contract. Cam Little, Trey Benson, Brian Robinson, Charlie Kolar, Jack Strand, Jacob Saylors and Stefon Diggs all signed at the league minimum; Parker Washington, Chig Okonkwo, Boutte and Mayer did not, and Washington and Okonkwo in particular carry current-year money well clear of it.

The Okonkwo sequence is the worst thing in the file. He bought a tight end at the Free Agent Auction, then handed that tight end a multi-year deal at real current-year money, and Okonkwo grades a Replacement-level TE sitting behind a Replacement-level TE. He spent at the position he is weakest at and the position did not move.

He made {{f.team.0008.trades_count}} trades and the good ones are obvious. Kenneth Walker went to HammerTime for HammerTime's natural first-rounder next season — talent out, future capital in. The Gride deal that sent out the pick which became Jadarian Price and brought back Travis Etienne plus the pick which became KC Concepcion is straight talent-driven, and he won it. The three-way with C-Town Chivalry and Blake Bombers cost him McMillan, his own natural first for next season, Chris Rodriguez and Omar Cooper for Nacua: pure talent consolidation, and note that Drake London and blind-bid consideration moved between the other two franchises, not through him.

Two of the six were pick-shuffles up his own board: he spent a future third to move up in the second round and take De'Zhaun Stribling, and spent two third-rounders to move up and take Sonny Styles. The Hawks deal is the odd one — he gave up George Karlaftis, a startable defensive lineman, plus a future fifth, to move up to a future fourth. Defensive line is the one place a wire genuinely restocks, so paying with a starter there is defensible; paying with a starter there for one round of draft position is thin. Across all of it he did not lose a first-rounder, he swapped which one he owns.

Contracts carried into the league year and then released came to {{f.team.0008.cuts_count}}. Noah Fant was tight end depth, Keon Coleman is a Replacement-level WR and was not contributing, Blake Watson was on the taxi and his salary never touched the cap, and Trey Benson was running-back depth — cut at a mid-range salary, penalty paid, then re-signed off the wire at the league minimum, which is a competent bit of price resetting. None of the five removed a starter. The penalty charged against this season is {{f.team.0008.cuts_penalty_2026}}, with {{f.team.0008.cuts_penalty_2027_deferred}} landing next season instead.

The rest of the churn is churn: {{f.team.0008.waiver_swaps}} of the drops were the make-room leg of a claim, {{f.team.0008.inyear_flyers}} bodies were signed and discarded inside the same offseason, and removals of all kinds totalled {{f.team.0008.roster_removals_total}}. He was busy. Busy is not the same as right, but nothing in that column cost him anything.

The rookie class ran to {{f.team.0008.rookie_picks_count}} picks. Concepcion, taken in the first round, comes from a slot where history says the pick is usable more often than not, and he currently grades a High-end WR3 on the bench. Omar Cooper Jr. came later in the same round from a slot with a roughly even historical band, grades a Replacement-level WR, and was included in the Nacua deal. Stribling — the second-rounder he traded up for — comes from a slot where history says usable rarely, and grades a Low-end WR3, which for a player with no games played is ahead of the band. Styles and Zion Young are defenders: no valuation source has an opinion on either yet, which is a gap in the measuring, not a mark against the picks.

captions.t.0008.contracts: One re-based deal, a stack of minimum signings, and two tight-end-adjacent prices that stand out.
captions.t.0008.trades: Six deals: two big talent moves, two board climbs, one pick nudge that cost a starter.
captions.t.0008.cuts: Depth and non-contributors only, and the deferred penalty is not this year's problem.
captions.t.0008.rookies: Pre-outcome expectation at each slot, next to what the market thinks of the player today.

paragraphs: Creelman does not have the strongest team in the league, and the composite says so at {{f.team.0008.composite_rank}}. He did have one of the more productive offseasons anyone ran, which is a separate question and a friendlier answer. Almost every priced starter he will use arrived this year.

The single biggest advantage is Nacua, an Elite WR1, with Parker Washington in a flex and Harrison Jr in reserve, and the receiver group grading {{f.team.0008.wr_rank}}. The single biggest weakness is tight end: Goedert starting and Okonkwo behind him, both Replacement-level TEs, one of them on money that should have bought something, and the position grading {{f.team.0008.te_rank}}. He bought four quarterbacks at one auction and the position still grades {{f.team.0008.qb_rank}}.

Barkley, Etienne and Henderson give him a backfield grading {{f.team.0008.rb_rank}}, which is the quietly fine part of this. The verdict is a good offseason attached to a middling team, and the reason is that he solved five holes down to two and then kept shopping at quarterback instead of at tight end. Nacua wins him games. Goedert is still there.
